chief_complaint: severe morning sickness, uterine enlargement greater than dates, and snowstorm pattern on ultrasound at 10 weeks
hpi_details: 23F at 10 weeks gestation presenting with hyperemesis gravidarum, vaginal bleeding with grape-like vesicles, beta-hCG markedly elevated (>150,000 mIU/mL), and TVUS showing diffuse vesicular snowstorm/honeycomb pattern without fetus requiring suction curettage.
ideas: She thinks she might be carrying twins or triplets because her belly has grown so quickly and her nausea is so intense.
concerns: She is worried that passing the grape-like tissue means she has lost the baby and will never be able to carry a healthy pregnancy.
expectations: She hopes to see her baby's heartbeat on the ultrasound and receive IV fluids to relieve her severe vomiting.

available_results.value: Diffuse vesicular snowstorm-pattern intrauterine tissue without an identifiable fetus
available_results.note: Consistent with a complete hydatidiform mole.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Hydatidiform mole (gestational trophoblastic disease) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Hydatidiform mole (gestational trophoblastic disease) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Hydatidiform Mole, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: At 10 weeks, hyperemesis, vaginal bleeding with passage of grape-like vesicles, and uterine size greater than dates are classic clinical features of a complete mole.
Markedly elevated quantitative beta-hCG (>150,000 mIU/mL) supports trophoblastic overgrowth and can cause hyperemesis or hyperthyroid symptoms.
Transvaginal ultrasound showing diffuse echogenic vesicular (snowstorm/honeycomb) intrauterine tissue without a fetus is characteristic of a complete hydatidiform mole.
Assess hemodynamic status and obtain CBC, blood type/Rh and screen, renal/liver function, and thyroid tests when symptoms or markedly elevated hCG suggest complications.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Hydatidiform mole (gestational trophoblastic disease).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Missed abortion without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Beta-hCG >150,000.
management_principles: Stabilize active bleeding, dehydration, and severe vomiting; evaluate for anemia, preeclampsia, hyperthyroidism, and other hCG-mediated complications before evacuation.
Arrange prompt uterine evacuation by suction dilation and curettage with pathology; give Rho(D) immune globulin to an unsensitized Rh-negative patient.
Obtain a baseline quantitative hCG after evacuation and follow serial hCG to documented remission using the local gestational trophoblastic disease surveillance protocol.
Counsel on reliable contraception during surveillance and urgently refer to gynecologic oncology for plateauing or rising hCG, which may indicate postmolar gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Gestational Trophoblastic Disease Hydatidiform Mole: severe morning sickness, uterine enlargement greater than dates, and snowstorm pattern on ultrasound at 10 weeks. 23F at 10 weeks gestation presenting with hyperemesis gravidarum, vaginal bleeding with grape-like vesicles, beta-hCG markedly elevated (>150,000 mIU/mL), and TVUS showing diffuse vesicular snowstorm/honeycomb pattern without fetus requiring suction curettage.
reference_soap.objective: Quantitative beta-hCG exceeds 150,000 mIU/mL, and transvaginal ultrasound shows diffuse vesicular intrauterine tissue without a fetus, consistent with a complete hydatidiform mole. Obtain CBC, blood type and screen, renal/liver tests, thyroid testing when clinically indicated, and baseline chest imaging according to local protocol.
reference_soap.assessment: Suspected complete hydatidiform mole with hyperemesis and vaginal bleeding.
reference_soap.plan: Stabilize bleeding and hyperemesis, arrange prompt suction dilation and curettage with pathology, and administer Rho(D) immune globulin if Rh-negative. Follow quantitative hCG after evacuation until negative and then at the recommended surveillance interval; advise reliable contraception during surveillance and refer promptly for plateauing or rising hCG suggestive of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

history.answer: I am ten weeks pregnant, but I have been throwing up nonstop for the past two weeks and cannot keep anything down.
The severe nausea and vomiting began about two weeks ago and has gotten progressively worse every single day.
I am vomiting six to seven times every day, usually throwing up within ten to twenty minutes after trying to eat or drink.
It is mostly clear fluid, stomach acid, and yellowish bile, with no frank blood or coffee-ground material.
I feel extremely nauseated first thing in the morning on an empty stomach, but the vomiting is not forceful or projectile.
I have a dull, heavy ache low down in my pelvis, but throwing up does not make that cramping go away.
My bowel movements have been slightly sluggish, but I am still passing gas and definitely do not have any diarrhea.
I have had no fever, chills, or sweating, and my husband ate the exact same food as me and feels completely fine.
No, I have not had any severe headaches, neck stiffness, blurry vision, or fainting spells.
No, I have not bumped my head or had any kind of injury recently.
I can barely keep even small sips of water down, my mouth is parched, and I only urinate once or twice a day with very dark urine.
No, I do not have diabetes, I have never taken insulin, and I do not have excessive thirst or urination.
I have not had any chest pain, shortness of breath, or coughing.
I do not drink alcohol, smoke marijuana, or use any recreational drugs, and I have not started any new prescription medications.
I have lost about four kilograms over the past two weeks because I cannot keep any food in my stomach.
No, absolutely not; I want to keep food down for the baby, so I would never make myself throw up on purpose.
Over the last four or five days, I noticed dark brown, prune juice-colored spotting that turned into intermittent bleeding.
Yesterday, when I wiped, I noticed small, clear, grape-like blisters coming out with the blood.
My lower belly feels unusually swollen and tight, as if I were already four or five months pregnant rather than just ten weeks.
My heart sometimes races when I stand up, but I have not had heat intolerance, hand tremors, or unusual sweating.
My last menstrual period started exactly ten weeks ago, my cycles have always been regular every twenty-eight days, and this is my first pregnancy.
I am married and sexually active with my husband, and we were actively trying to conceive so we were not using contraception.
I have never had any chronic medical conditions, high blood pressure, or thyroid disease.
I have never had any surgeries, and I have never been admitted to a hospital before.
I only took an over-the-counter prenatal vitamin, but I had to stop taking it several days ago because it made me vomit immediately.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used e-cigarettes.
I do not drink alcohol at all, especially now that I am pregnant.
I work as an office administrator and live in an apartment with my husband.
There is no history of pregnancy complications, abnormal pregnancies, or gynecological cancers in my family.
I thought maybe I was having twins or triplets because my stomach got big so fast and the sickness has been so overwhelming.

I'm terrified that passing those strange clusters means my baby is gone and I'll never be able to carry a pregnancy. I really hope you can check for the baby's heartbeat on the ultrasound and give me an IV to stop this constant vomiting.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 108/68 mmHg, heart rate is 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, and temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius.
Oral mucosa and lips appear dry, with no pharyngeal injection or tonsillar swelling.
Decreased skin turgor with slightly dry skin and a capillary refill time under two seconds.
The lower abdomen appears visibly fuller and more prominent than expected for a ten-week gestation.
Normoactive bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants.
The uterine fundus is palpable midway between the pubic symphysis and umbilicus, measuring roughly fourteen to sixteen weeks in size, with mild discomfort on deep palpation.
No rebound tenderness or involuntary abdominal muscle guarding is elicited.
Speculum examination reveals dark brownish blood and small clusters of translucent grape-like vesicles in the vaginal vault, with a closed external cervical os.
Thyroid gland is normal in size and non-tender, with no palpable nodules or bruits.
No resting, postural, or action tremor is observed in the outstretched hands.
Neck is supple with full range of motion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
